ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: Snorri himself — the man who wrote down Norse mythology — was **murdered in his own cellar at Reykholt on 23 September 1241**, on the orders of the Norwegian king, by a raiding party led by **Gizur Þorvaldsson, his own former son-in-law**. His last words: ***"Eigi skal höggva!"*** — "Don't strike!" They struck.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age

en: Weather pivot (if the eruption is invisible): "Even in thick fog you'll still hear Strokkur go off and feel the ground tense up first — the one geyser that named all the others doesn't need you to see it to make its point."

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: The original **Geysir** is first recorded in **1294**, when earthquakes reshaped the field's springs — at its peak it threw water **60–80 m** up. It's mostly **dormant** now, but its reliable cousin **Strokkur** ("the Churn") goes **every 6–10 minutes**, **15–20 m** high (occasionally 40).

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: Watch the **dome** bulge just before it fires: a thin layer of cooler water over near-boiling water below, pressure building until it punches through.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: The field sits on the **Hreppar block** — water seeps down, hits **200°C+ rock**, flashes to steam, shoots back up.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: **Geysir runs on earthquakes.** Born in the annals after the **1294** quakes, it roars back after every big southern shake — **1630**, **1896**, most recently **June 2000** — then dozes off again between them, sometimes for decades.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: Icelanders never quite accepted the naps: they used to **shovel rocks and turf in** to provoke it, and from **1963 to 1981** the official trick was **soap** — lower the surface tension and the superheated water boils over. The country literally **washed its geyser into performing**. (We've since let it sleep with dignity.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: The name **Geysir** (from *geysa*, "to gush") first appears in writing in **1647** — and as Enlightenment scientists took an interest, the word spread to **every language on Earth**, all from this one field.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: At its most active it took **8 to 10 hours** to refill between eruptions. In **1896** it came back erupting **several times a day**, then fell dormant around **1915**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: A **channel was cut in 1935** to lower the water surface and restart it, then **re-cut and deepened in 1981**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: **Strokkur** is straight thermodynamics: **one metre down the water is 90–95°C**, at **ten metres 112°C**, and at the bottom of the **23-metre shaft about 130°C** — held liquid only by the weight of water above it. Take the lid off and it flashes to steam.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: Measured eruptions in **2000** threw between about **270 and 425 litres** of water, or **300 to 500 litres** once you count what leaves as steam.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: **Strokkur's** reliability is younger than most of its audience. Its nineteenth-century performances are said to have **lasted an hour and reached up to 60 metres** — then it fell silent for decades. In **1963** the decision was taken to **drill about 40 metres into the gosskál**, the eruption basin, and it has been **extraordinarily active** ever since. The most dependable natural spectacle in this country is not entirely natural.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: One more number for the shaft: a **cold vein comes in at about 13 metres** down. That is part of why height, duration and interval all vary — and why nobody will ever hand you a timetable, so keep looking at the water rather than at your phone.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
en: In **1907** an Englishman leased the falls from farmer **Tómas Tómasson** for a **hydro plant**. His daughter **Sigríður Tómasdóttir** spent her own savings on a Reykjavík lawyer — **Sveinn Björnsson**, later Iceland's **first president** — and fought for years to void the lease. The famous "walked barefoot to Reykjavík / threatened to jump" details are **romanticised**; she genuinely **lost in court**, but the lease then **lapsed because the developers stopped paying the rent**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
en: Gullfoss survived, became a **nature reserve in 1979**, and Sigríður — remembered on a memorial above the falls — is now called **Iceland's first environmentalist**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
en: The gorge below runs about **2.5 km long and 70 m deep**, and mean flow over the lip is **109 m³/s**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
en: The Englishman's offer, early in **1907**, was **50,000 krónur** — and Iceland passed a law that same year restricting **foreign ownership of waterfalls**, after which foreign parties obtained rental rights anyway.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
en: **Sigríður Tómasdóttir**, **1871 to 1957**, came from the farm **Brattholt** above the falls, and what she spent years trying to void were the agreements **her own father had signed**. The judgement went against the Brattholt family.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
en: What actually saved it was duller than the legend: in **1928** the rental payments stopped and the agreement fell void. The reserve declaration was signed on **9 March 1979** and covers **164.2 hectares**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
en: Her lawyer was **Sveinn Björnsson**, who went on to become Iceland's first president, **1944 to 1952**. (Losing that case turned out to be quite good for his CV.)

en: The **Icelandic horse** is small (**~132–145 cm**), shaggy, long-lived (often **30 years**), tough and frankly opinionated — and by breed convention and national insistence, **always a "horse," never a pony**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

Minjastofnun's phrase for the place is the **head place of Iceland for about 700 years**, and the bishopric ran **continuously from 1056 to 1801**, moving to **Reykjavík** only in the wake of the great natural disasters at the end of the eighteenth century.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⚡ Sog River
en: The consequence was entirely domestic. **Ljósafoss quadrupled the electricity available to the capital region**, and **Reykjavík households swapped their coal ranges for electric cookers.** A whole city stopped smelling of smoke because of a drop in a river almost none of them had ever visited. **Steingrímsstöð** very nearly did not happen either — its dam **gave way during construction in the storm of 17 June 1959.** Losing a dam on the national day is not a detail Icelanders bring up often.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⚡ Sog River

en: The **Garðyrkjuskóli ríkisins** at **Reykir** — the state horticultural college — turned out **its first qualified horticulturists in the spring of 1941**, and most of them went straight out and built nurseries of their own here. The count tells it better than any adjective could: **seven horticultural stations in Hveragerði by 1940, twenty by 1950.** Flower growing took off across the forties and the place became **blómabærinn**, the flower town.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **about 3,350 today, 3,344 at the start of 2026.** The name is far older than the town. **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing.**

en: Veðurstofa Íslands logged the 2008 quake to the minute — **fimmtudaginn 29. maí kl. 15:45**, announced that afternoon at magnitude **6.3** (the Met Office's English release settles on **6.1** for the composite event), epicentre at **Ingólfsfjall in Ölfus, about 5 km north-west of Selfoss**, with a very large number of aftershocks behind it. ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: We're on the **Hengill volcanic system**, a rare **plate-boundary triple junction on dry land**. Water goes down, returns at nearly **300°C**, and spins turbines — the white plumes are **steam**, not smoke. Built up in stages 2006–2011 to **303 MW**, it's **Iceland's largest geothermal power station**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: After the electricity, the leftover hot water pipes off to heat **more than half of the capital region** — nothing wasted.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Via **CarbFix**, CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped into hot basalt, where **~95% turns to solid rock within about two years** (Matter et al., 2016). Next door, **Climeworks' Mammoth** plant (2024) sucks CO₂ straight from the air — up to **36,000 tonnes a year** — for the same rock treatment.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: The trick that makes the whole thing work: the geothermal fluid under us is **hot, corrosive and loaded with dissolved minerals**, and it never goes anywhere near your radiator. It is used to **heat clean groundwater through heat exchangers**, and that clean heated water is what travels to the city. **You get the heat without the chemistry.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Hellisheiði's quieter half is the hot water: **200 MW of thermal output**, about **950 litres per second** down the pipe. Over the ridge sits its older sibling **Nesjavellir** — **Reykjavík bought the farm in 1965** and production still did not begin until **1990**, which is **twenty-five years** of drilling, testing and arguing before one useful litre went anywhere. It now runs at **up to 120 MW of electricity** and **up to 300 MW of thermal**, or as Orka náttúrunnar puts it in the only unit a household understands: **1,640 litres of hot water every second.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Nesjavellir has grown hard. In the late **1990s** the same station was being reported to Alþingi at **60 MW of electricity and 200 MW of heat** — **the electrical output has since doubled and the heat output is up by half**, on the same hillside, with the same rock. Between the two stations, **Orka náttúrunnar supplies roughly 60 per cent of all the hot water in the capital region.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: **Hengill** is not a peak, it is a **volcanic system 50 to 60 kilometres long** and **5 to 10 kilometres wide**, running from **Selvogur** in the south-west all the way up to **Þingvallavatn**. Its most recent eruptions, about **1,900 years ago**, produced **Nesjahraun** and part of **Hellisheiðarhraun**; an earlier round **5,700 to 5,800 years ago** produced **Hagavíkurhraun**. It is **classified as active** — and this power station was built on that basis, not in spite of it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Nationally, **about 90 per cent of the energy used to heat Icelandic homes comes from geothermal** — that is Orkustofnun's figure for **2020.** The comparable British number is effectively **zero.**
